3.Section 1367(d) includes a tolling provision that enables a party to refile state claims in state court after some claims asserted under Section
1367(a) are dismissed. In JINKS v. RICHLAND COUNTY, S.C., 538 U.S. 456, 123 S.Ct. 1667, 155 L.Ed.2d 631 (2003), the Supreme Court held
that the statute’s tolling of the state statute of limitations while the original lawsuit was pending in federal court was not unconstitutional, but rather was
necessary and proper for the fair and efficient administration of the federal courts. In ARTIS v. DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA, 583 U.S. ___, 138 S.Ct.
594, 199 L.Ed.2d 473 (2018), the Court, five-to-four, held that the provision stops the clock on the state statute of limitations, thus suspending the
limitations period while the federal action is pending and for 30 days after dismissal. Justice Gorsuch, in a dissenting opinion joined by Justices
Kennedy, Thomas, and Alito, interpreted the provision as affording the plaintiff, after a dismissal of the party’s state law claim without a ruling on the
merits, “whatever time state law allows, or at least 30 days, to refile the claim in state court.” Id. at ___, 138 S.Ct. at 608, 199 L.Ed.2d at 490.
NOTE ON NONSTATUTORY ANCILLARY JURISDICTION
After the codification of pendent and ancillary jurisdiction in 28 U.S.C. § 1367, do federal courts retain any inherent authority to exercise
jurisdiction when it is not conferred by statute? This question was presented in KOKKONEN v. GUARDIAN LIFE INSURANCE CO. OF
AMERICA, 511 U.S. 375, 114 S.Ct. 1673, 128 L.Ed.2d 391 (1994). The action involved a dispute between an insurer and an insurance agent for
breach of an agency agreement. The action was filed in state court and removed to federal court on the basis of diversity jurisdiction. Pursuant to
Federal Rule 41(a)(1)(ii), the parties executed a Stipulation and Order of Dismissal, which the district court signed. Later, a dispute arose about the
settlement agreement, and the insurer moved to enforce that agreement. The district court entered an enforcement order asserting it had “inherent
authority” to do so, rejecting the argument that it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over the settlement. The court of appeals affirmed, and the Supreme
Court reversed and remanded. Significantly, the Supreme Court acknowledged that a residual category of ancillary jurisdiction—“over some matters
(otherwise beyond their competence) that are incidental to other matters properly before them”—survives the enactment of 28 U.S.C. § 1367.
